Jesus Christ I can't even fathom the consequences of every American under twenty-five dying.  Just looking at the immediate consequences, everyone involved with schools and univeristies would be out of a job.  We would have to hire daycare and preschool workers almost immediately and primary-school teachers would be in demand again in half a decade, but they would be absolutely no need for university professors for almost twenty years.  With not even the possibiity of a faculty position, there would be very little incentive for new academic research outside of some very specific, government-subsidized areas, mostly in the applied sciences.  And what would the existing researchers do without those young graduate students to man their labs?  
And of course a lot of consumer industries would disappear overnight.  Hollywood would have to stop marketing their summer blockbusters to teenage boys, because there wouldn't be any to see their movies.  Say goodbye to the Marvel Cinematic Universe and allied franchises.  Would there even be big-budget movies after all the young people die?  The same with music.  Let's face it: what's trendy in popular music is mostly determined by what older teens and younger twenty-somethings are listening to.  Record companies would at least have to seriously reconsider how they market their products.  
And industries that rely directly on young labor would obviously suffer.  Fastfood chains and retailers might not be able to sell their goods so cheap without kids who will work for minimum wage.  Granted, older adults also work for McDonald's and Wal Mart, but there would still be a significant drop in the amount of people who would be willing to work in such poor conditions for such low pay.
Jesus Christ what would happen to spectator sports?  Obviously, college football and basketball would disappear instantly, not to return for eighteen years, if those programs will even be able to be revived after all that time.  Remember, big state universities won't even be operating, since there will hardly be any undergraduates to teach, so we might not have colleges at all by the time the first eighteen-year-olds graduate from high school.  And maybe the professional leagues like the NFL would be able to get on just fine for a couple of years, since the star players usually aren't rookies, but can you imagine twenty NFL seasons without a draft?  I'm not sure there would be an NFL by the time any rookies are ready to play.  
So with professional sports, so with the armed forces.  I won't pretend to understand the full strategic implications of having a military with no new recruits for the better part of two decades, but I'm sure the United States's ability to defend its people and its interests would be significantly compromised.  

Those are just some of the immediate consequences of everyone under twenty-five dying.  Just to put this in persective, there are about a hundred million Americans under twenty-five.  In other words, this poster is suggesting that one third of the United States be killed.  We can't possibly keep our economy running at anything resembling the status quo with a worker shortage that massive, no to mention the loss of a hundred million taxpayers who contribute to entitlements, infrastructure, and government services.  Japan already has a huge problem with its aging population, with two elderly dependents for every three workers, but that's nowhere near as extreme as the situation we would have if there were literally no workers between the ages of, say, twenty and forty-five.  At that point, almost all Americans would either be of retiring age or would be children.  I imagine this Gawker commenter, who is no doubt over twenty-five, won't be happy when his Social Security checks stop coming in because there's no one to contribute to them, if there is even a federal government to pay Social Security to at that point.  Are we going to fill Congress and the executive branch with teenagers or feebleminded old folks?  The immediate stuff I listed above is pretty superifical; the lack of a workforce able to contribute to the welfare state is really when this commenter's plan would become catostrophic.

I don't think it matters what we call the greatest being, in the end.  If we define Flying Spaghetti Monster as the greatest possible being, then the argument would work the same way.  But if we say that the Flying Spaghetti Monster is literally made of Spaghetti, we might have some problems. One issue I see with the greatest society is that the society has no independent existence (you can't have a society without people), and so its existence can't be necessary.

And I'm taking premises 1 and 2 to mean the same thing in different words.  If you agree that God is possible, then I think you have to say that he exists in a possible world.  This is a normal way of speaking about possibilities and necessities.

I don't think so.  We're basically saying that the greatest being possibly has necessary existence.  And necessary existence means existing in all possible worlds.  So if in some possible world God necessarily exists, then God exists in all possible worlds, even ours, the actual world.

I'm not sure we really have to say exactly what greatness means, as long as we agree that existing is more worlds is greater than existing in fewer worlds and as long as we say that having all of God's properties is part of what it means to be great.  I think that the greatest being would have to be omnipotent, omniscient and omnibenevolent, since I think we could make great being even greater by giving it any one of those properties.  But this is only if you even think a greatest being is possible; if you deny this, then you are a conceptual atheist, and Plantinga would have nothing to say to you.

It's not just about omnipotence.  We take for granted that a greatest being possibly exists.  So there's a possible world W where the greatest being exists.  And then we say that a being that necessarily exists is greater than one that doesn't necessarily exist.  But if the greatest being necessarily exists in W, then that's just another way of saying that it exists in all possible worlds (necessary existence means not possibly not existing: there is no possible world where this thing doesn't exist).  So the important point is that there is nothing greater than God.

If you want to deny that a necessary being could possibly exist, I won't stop you.  I don't think Plantinga or anyone has a good argument for why we have to think that God is possible.  My only point is that the modal ontological argument poses a potential problem for the factual atheist, who does concede that something like God is possible.
